assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance programme changed how economists treat institutions, investor protection and financial development. It created a durable empirical research agenda across corporate finance, comparative law and development, and it has had wide policy influence.
assessment.attribution: The core papers are jointly authored by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny. Shleifer, La Porta and Lopez-de-Silanes are the most consistent common authors across the legal-origins and investor-protection work. Vishny is a real contributor, especially on the earlier papers, so the three-person limit leaves out a legitimate claimant.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the late 1990s, so it has had about 25 years to be tested, extended and criticised. The timing is mature.
uncertainties: The legal-origins thesis has been challenged on causal identification and on the coding of legal variables.
Choosing which of the four co-authors to credit is a judgement call.
Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize may make the committee cautious about thematic repetition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the measurement of trade shocks reshaped understanding of labour demand, polarisation and wage inequality. The research has been influential in both academic and policy debates.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Katz are central to the skill-biased change and task-model line of work. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are central to the China-shock papers. Hanson links the two strands in the three-person group, but this leaves out Dorn and Acemoglu-style task theory, which the list does not credit here.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly 1998 to the 2010s and is well established. The China-shock results are still being refined.
uncertainties: The empirical estimates and long-run interpretation of the China shock are still debated.
Overlap with recent prizes on labour economics and technology and growth may count against it.
The three-name limit forces an arbitrary exclusion, most visibly of Dorn.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top incomes and wealth transformed the empirical study of inequality and public debate about taxation. The work also opened a data-building programme that many researchers now follow.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the principal originators of the top-incomes series, with Piketty also credited for the long-run wealth framework. Zucman contributed offshore wealth and distributional accounts, but his work is more recent.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work dates from the early 2000s and is mature. The wealth and offshore strands are newer and still being evaluated.
uncertainties: Measurement choices and the theoretical conclusions in the wealth-inequality work have been criticised.
The prize may be seen as favouring data and measurement over identified causal mechanisms.
How to weigh Zucman's more recent contribution is unsettled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The firm-heterogeneity framework shifted trade theory from representative-firm models to selection, exporters and within-industry reallocation. It underlies much of modern empirical trade and has had a large influence on policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 paper is the clear origin of the heterogeneous-firm model. Helpman has the broader record, with Helpman–Melitz–Yeaple on exports versus foreign direct investment and earlier foundational trade theory. Redding is an important extender, but his contribution is less foundational.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from about 2003 and has had two decades of theoretical and empirical development. Credit is clear for the core model.
uncertainties: Krugman's earlier prize on new trade theory may affect how the committee views trade topics.
Other heterogeneous-firm contributors, such as Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, are not credited here.
Quantitative implications for gains from trade are model-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics gave a formal, empirically testable account of how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal and growth outcomes. It unified theory and evidence in an area previously left to political science.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central joint authors on constitutions and policy outcomes. Besley is central to state capacity and political agency. The three-person group is coherent and well delimited.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and 2000s and is well established. The Persson–Tabellini and Besley lines have been extended widely.
uncertainties: Causal identification for the effects of constitutional rules is limited.
The 2024 institutions prize may reduce appetite for another prize on political economy.
Other founders of political economy, such as Alesina and Acemoglu–Robinson, are outside this list, so the credit boundary is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model is a cornerstone of non-cooperative game theory. It supplies the micro-foundations for bargaining, market search and many applied models, and it influences mechanism and market design.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein's 1982 paper is the clear origin of the model. Binmore and Wolinsky made important contributions, notably the market-bargaining extensions and the link to Nash's solution, but the foundational credit is concentrated in one person.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 1982 and is very mature. Its importance has been clear for decades.
uncertainties: Stahl's related work and Nash and Selten's earlier prizes complicate how credit is distributed.
A solo award may leave out other contributors to market bargaining.
The strategic-bargaining model may be seen as primarily theoretical, with a long gap since its introduction.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Social-preference models explain behaviour in ultimatum, public-goods and trust games, and they offer a tractable way to introduce fairness into economic theory. The work links experiments to theory and has had a wide influence.
assessment.attribution: The Fehr–Schmidt inequity-aversion model of 1999 is the defining theoretical contribution. Fehr's experimental programme on reciprocity and punishment is the broader body of work. Falk is a major collaborator, but his is a secondary contribution.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 1999 and the surrounding work spans about 25 years. Applications continue.
uncertainties: Rabin, Bolton–Ockenfels and others made parallel contributions to fairness models.
The external validity of laboratory evidence is debated, as is replication of some results.
Prior behavioural prizes (Kahneman and Smith, Thaler) may affect the committee's appetite for this area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design created a tractable framework for how a sender chooses an information structure to influence decisions. It connects to mechanism design, communication and applied policy and has had a large influence on theory.
assessment.attribution: The 2011 Kamenica–Gentzkow paper is the canonical origin. Bergemann and Morris built the broader information-design and robust-mechanism literature. Credit would need to be shared between the persuasion origin and the information-design generalisation.
assessment.maturity: The origin paper is about 15 years old. The literature is large and still developing, so it is less mature than the higher-ranked candidates.
uncertainties: The field is young relative to typical prize timing, and the empirical record of applications is thin.
Deciding whether credit belongs to the persuasion origin or the broader Bergemann–Morris line is difficult.
Gentzkow's other empirical work, which is not part of the persuasion contribution, may blur how the prize is framed.
